exam.label: Question 1
exam.stem: Comprehensively explain the concept of international entrepreneurship and innovation along with their significance to the global economy. In your answer, include:
paperParts: The definition of international entrepreneurship according to Zahra & George (2002) and Oviatt & McDougall (2005).
The difference between International New Ventures (INVs) and Born Globals.
At least two statistical data showing the contribution of immigrant entrepreneurs to the economy (e.g., from USBA, NVCA, or OECD).
Real examples of companies founded by immigrants and their impact on global innovation.

stops.name: Border
stops.text: International entrepreneurship is where two fields meet: entrepreneurship and international business. [[Zahra and George]] (2002) define it as creatively discovering and exploiting opportunities [[outside a firm's domestic market]] to gain [[competitive advantage]]. This tells us where the opportunity is and why the firm wants it. [[Oviatt and McDougall]] (2005) define it as the [[discovery, enactment, evaluation and exploitation]] of opportunities [[across national borders]] to create future goods and services. This tells us how it happens.

This tells us how it happens.

stops.name: Engine
stops.text: Innovation is the engine of this process. [[Drucker]] (1993) says innovation is [[creativity plus commercialization]]. [[Schumpeter]] adds that innovations create new demand, which destroys old markets and creates new ones. This is why the field matters to the global economy: it carries innovation across borders.

stops.name: Day One
stops.text: Some firms go international very early. [[INVs]] (Oviatt & McDougall, 1994) are firms that, from the start, seek competitive advantage by using resources and selling in [[many countries]]. A [[born global]] is a firm launched to serve a [[global niche]] from its first day (Tanev, 2012).† So the difference is simple. An INV is known by where it uses resources and sells. A born global is known by the global niche it is built around.

In the US, innovative start-ups founded by immigrants made up as many as [[50%]] of gross jobs created each year between 1980 and 2010 (NVCA, 2019).

stops.name: Names
stops.text: [[Uber and eBay]] were founded by immigrants and built new markets. In [[Southern California]], firms founded by Chinese and Taiwanese Americans employ more than [[440,000]] people. They also helped develop China's technology industries, so innovation flowed back across borders. In conclusion, international entrepreneurship matters because it spreads innovation and creates jobs and wealth across countries, and migration is a major source of that innovation.

exam.label: Question 2
exam.stem: Analyze the role of small firms in a country's economy using entrepreneurship theories (Personality Theory, Psycho-sociological Theory, Cognitive Theories). In your answer:
paperParts: Explain the difference between entrepreneurship and small business.
Elaborate on the advantages and disadvantages of small firms from quantitative and qualitative aspects.
Provide arguments on why small firms are often called the backbone of job creation in the United States, including data from USBA (2018).
Relate it to Schumpeter's concept of creative destruction.

stops.name: Shop
stops.text: Small firms help a country's economy because entrepreneurs use them to create jobs, wealth and innovation. Entrepreneurship and small business are not the same. [[Entrepreneurship]] is about starting up, where innovative effort is needed. [[Small business]] is about established small firms, like a corner grocery or a laundromat. A small business has [[fewer than 500]] employees and sells less than [[$5 million]] a year.

stops.name: Three Doors
stops.text: Three theories explain why people start firms. [[Personality theory]] says it comes from who you are: entrepreneurs are "born", not "made". [[Psycho-sociological theory]] says people can be pushed: being unhappy in a job, or "disgruntlement", can be the trigger. [[Cognitive theories]] say entrepreneurs spot market gaps that others have not noticed.

stops.name: Balance
stops.text: In numbers (quantitative), small firms have few employees, little starting capital, low turnover and a small market. In character (qualitative), they have an informal culture, family often plays a role, and the owner is also the manager. This cuts both ways. The advantages are motivation and energy, an informal structure and [[closeness to the market]]. The disadvantages are no [[economies of scale]], limited money and people, and no control over the market.

stops.name: Backbone
stops.text: Small firms are called the backbone of job creation in the US, and the data show why. According to [[USBA]] (2018), [[30.2 million]] small businesses make up [[99.7%]] of US firms with paid employees and employ [[47.5%]] of private sector workers. In 2018, they provided [[55%]] of all jobs and [[66%]] of all net new jobs.

stops.name: Wrecking Ball
stops.text: [[Schumpeter's]] creative destruction shows they do more than give jobs. An invention is a new idea. It becomes an innovation when it is used in a new product or service. Entrepreneurs bring it to market and it creates new demand. New demand [[destroys old markets]] and creates new ones, which brings wealth and jobs. In conclusion, small firms are not only employers. They also change the economy.

exam.label: Question 3
exam.stem: Based on the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) 2018 data, answer the following:
paperParts: Explain what the Total Entrepreneurial Activity (TEA) Index is and how it is measured.
Analyze the differences in entrepreneurial motivation (opportunity vs necessity entrepreneurs) in low-, middle-, and high-income countries.
Elaborate on the U-shaped relationship between the level of entrepreneurial activity and a country's economic development.
Discuss how political, economic, socio-cultural, and technological factors influence the development of international entrepreneurship, referring to Hofstede's cultural dimensions.

stops.name: Gauge
stops.text: [[TEA]] means Total Entrepreneurial Activity. It is the percentage of adults who have taken some action to create a new business in the past year, or who own and manage an active business less than [[42 months]] old. It is measured by adding two rates: the [[nascent start-up rate]] and the [[new business ownership rate]]. GEM 2018 shows rates from a few per cent in Japan to around [[40%]] in Angola.

stops.name: Motive
stops.text: TEA shows how many people start a business, but not why. [[Opportunity]] entrepreneurs start a business to use an opportunity. [[Necessity]] entrepreneurs start one because they have no other good work options. The share of opportunity entrepreneurs rises from [[37%]] in low-income countries to [[42%]] in middle-income and [[51%]] in high-income countries.

stops.name: The U
stops.text: GEM finds [[no causal link]] between entrepreneurial activity and GDP, but the relationship with development has a U shape. In low- and middle-income countries, activity is quite high and much of it comes from necessity, but it falls as incomes rise and jobs appear. In high-income countries, necessity is low, but [[opportunity entrepreneurship]] starts to grow, so activity rises again.

stops.name: Four Winds
stops.text: Politically, the type of system and government action matter, such as tax and regulation. Economically, the level of development shapes motivation. Socio-culturally, attitudes matter, such as the status of entrepreneurs. Technologically, information and communication technology connects entrepreneurs with [[international customers]], so they can sell outside their home market.

stops.name: Five Dials
stops.text: [[Hofstede]] (1991) describes national culture with five dimensions: [[power distance]], [[uncertainty avoidance]], [[individualism]], [[masculinity]] and [[long-term orientation]]. For example, low uncertainty avoidance suits the risk of starting a venture. But successful countries score very differently on each dimension, so there is no single "right" culture. In conclusion, income level shapes how many people start businesses and why, and the four factors work together.

exam.topic: Topic A: Local and Regional Dimensions of International Entrepreneurship
paperParts: Explain the concepts of regions and knowledge spillovers.
Elaborate on the role of human capital, social capital, and entrepreneurial capital in regional entrepreneurship development.
Analyze how growth corridors (e.g., Maputo Development Corridor) can connect local regions with cross-border regions and create transnational regions.
Provide real examples of regional clusters of entrepreneurship (e.g., Silicon Valley).

stops.name: Region
stops.text: International entrepreneurship grows in regions, not only in countries. A region is an area linked to policies and institutions that support economic development, social cohesion and environmental welfare. It is usually part of a country, a [[sub-national]] unit, but it can also cover several countries.

stops.name: Leak
stops.text: Knowledge spillovers are knowledge externalities [[bounded in space]]. In simple words, knowledge is "leaky", so rivals nearby can use some of it without creating it. This is why firms close to sources of knowledge can innovate faster. Knowledge moves in four ways: [[employees changing jobs]], [[universities]], [[informal collaborations]] and [[value chains]].

stops.text: People decide how well a region uses this knowledge. [[Human capital]] matters because places that attract talent also gain the ability to invent. The mix of these capitals is a good measure of how competitive a region is.

stops.name: Corridor
stops.text: Growth corridors are bundles of infrastructure, like rail links and highways, that connect urban areas in one country or in neighbouring countries. They grow in stages. [[Hard infrastructure]] creates a transport corridor. More traffic then needs [[soft infrastructure]], like logistics and legal support. Finally, efficiency attracts investment and creates an [[economic corridor]]. The first was the [[Maputo Development Corridor]], set up in 1996. Corridors link local regions with cross-border regions, and as investment grows, the connected regions work together as a [[transnational region]].

exam.topic: Topic B: Migration and Global Entrepreneurship
paperParts: Explain how international migration flows have fostered entrepreneurial activity.
Analyze migrant entrepreneurial trajectories using the concepts of dual habitus and dual contextual knowledge.
Discuss the challenges and barriers faced by migrant entrepreneurs, including refugee entrepreneurship.
Provide case examples of global migrant networks of innovation and their contributions to innovation and technology transfer.

stops.name: Suitcase
stops.text: Migration has become a major source of entrepreneurship. Migrants bring knowledge and skills from their [[country of origin]] and gain new abilities in their [[country of residence]]. Using these skills raises their motivation to start businesses in both countries. In most OECD countries, immigrants start businesses at the same rate as local people, and in some they are about [[1.5 times]] as likely to be self-employed.

stops.name: Two Shores
stops.text: [[Dual habitus]] explains this change. Migrants live between the country of destination and the country of origin. This gives them [[dual contextual knowledge]], empathy and access to resources in both. Knowing two places helps them see opportunities and serve customers in both. They also do not simply accept the rules of institutions. They actively shape them.

stops.text: Migrant entrepreneurs still face barriers. They are limited by [[home-country]] resources and institutions. [[Little is known]] about their networks and abilities. [[Policy makers]] do not pay enough attention to them. More detailed [[data]] is also needed. Refugees face these problems even more strongly. They can create wealth and jobs, but insecurity, legal rights and institutional issues make their position different. The word that best describes it is [[fragility]].

[[Uber and eBay]] are also immigrant-founded. In conclusion, migration fosters entrepreneurship by moving skills and resources between countries.
